This chapter presents the development of machine learning models for short-term energy demand forecasting in academic buildings, using a dataset from a higher education campus in Portugal. The dataset comprises quarter-hourly power demand data collected between January 2016 and February 2020, along with relevant exogenous variables. The study focuses on the impact of hyperparameter tuning on model performance, applying various algorithms—including Random Forest, Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines, Artificial Neural Network, and Support Vector Machines. Grid Search and Random Search techniques were employed to optimize each model’s hyperparameters. Performance was evaluated using benchmarking metrics and visualization tools such as daily load profiles and scatter plots. The results indicate that the Random Forest and Artificial Neural Network models outperformed the others, particularly during school days and examination periods, which represent the most active times on campus. Beyond its technical contributions, this chapter illustrates how machine learning-based forecasting can support energy-aware decision-making in academic buildings, contributing to more efficient and sustainable campus operations. Moreover, the case study presented here highlights the pedagogical potential of integrating AI tools into sustainability curricula, fostering interdisciplinary learning and providing students and researchers with practical insights into the application of artificial intelligence in real-world energy systems.

Trained machine learning models can hold on to traces of the data they were built from, including personal, outdated, incorrect, or unauthorized records. Deleting an entry from a database does not erase what a model has already absorbed from it. Machine unlearning tackles this gap by lowering or removing the effect of chosen training data, ideally without retraining the whole model every time. This review looks at five studies published between 2021 and 2025: one on coded machine unlearning, one on neuron masking, one on zero-shot unlearning, and two wider surveys of methods and evaluation. Together they trace a path from partition-based training designs and changes to model structure toward techniques that still work after the original training samples are gone, accompanied by increasingly systematic taxonomies and metrics. We compare the studies on the data access they assume, the unlearning strategy they use, their efficiency, how well they preserve utility, and how forgetting is verified. We also discuss the main open problems: the absence of a universal evaluation standard, the tension between forgetting and keeping performance on retained tasks, the risk of leftover information, and the difficulty of carrying these methods over to large language models and live systems. The work is a focused narrative review of the chosen papers; no new experiments or benchmark results are claimed. Our conclusion is that machine unlearning is a promising tool for privacy and model governance, but dependable use in practice requires measurable forgetting, clearly stated assumptions, and independent verification.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI is widely framed as democratizing skilled work by lowering the barrier to producing professional output. Drawing on 21 semi-structured interviews with 27 workers across 21 small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) in Kenya and Nigeria (July to October 2023), we find that availability alone did not make participation workable. In participants' accounts, drafting was rarely the hard part. The consequential work was making AI-assisted drafts defensible enough to circulate to clients. We identify five intertwined practices through which participants made generative AI workable: using it as draft labour, steering outputs through iterative interaction, switching and comparing across tools, performing release work to make outputs accountable before circulation, and repairing context misfit when outputs failed local requirements. We make two central contributions. First, we specify release work as a distinct, boundary-facing form of accountability labour, evidenced through verification gates, traceability reconstruction when sources fail, and non-delegation boundaries that decide what can ship. Second, we show how localization and representational failures, which we call context misfit, operate in everyday work as a recurring breakdown-and-repair class, including failures of local language, institutional knowledge, and the credible representation of African people and places, and we document the repair repertoire they demanded. Reframing democratization as workable participation, we argue that reported gains were conditional on this accountability and repair labour, and we translate the findings into four design directions for workplace generative AI. We treat Kenya and Nigeria as two situated cases, not as a representative sample of SMBs or the Global South.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Cinematic video generation requires both temporal inference from limited inputs (i.e., sparse rather than frame-by-frame guidance) and factor-aware control of character, scene, action, and camera. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer useful priors for both capabilities, but their representations are not automatically actionable for video generation: a Video Diffusion Transformer (DiT) may bypass them through native conditioning pathways, and using them does not ensure either factor-aware control or generation-compatible temporal prediction. We propose Factor-Aware Predictive Learning (FAPL), which establishes effective MLLM latent use as a shared prerequisite and then targets the two capabilities with complementary learning signals. First, latent-only generator grounding trains the DiT with a frozen MLLM and connector, strengthening the DiT's use of MLLM latents for generation. Second, for factor-aware control, paired videos specify a target-factor change and non-target preservation, and factor-span replacement trains the DiT to realize this relationship in its output. Third, for temporal inference, text-only and text-plus-complete-video observations share a video target, and the trained DiT is then frozen while the MLLM and connector are optimized through it. This final stage trains limited-input representations for generation while retaining complete-observation reconstruction as a complementary training mode. Extensive experiments demonstrate our consistently better performance on three cinematic video generation tasks (i.e., sparse-to-video, factor-aware editing, and multi-shot generation) over baselines and validate FAPL's contributions to MLLM feature use, temporal control, and factor coordination.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: The use of Conversational Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is growing as a way to interact with health information, especially for the public. This theory-based conceptual synthesis suggests a multilevel governance approach to reducing the likelihood for generated information to become unsafe action – GenAI health information resilience (GenAI-HIR). Its contribution is immediately usable and practical — deploying organizations and public-health actors and public-health actors can use the consequence-based control tiers, actor-specific safeguards, and domain-level audit anchors, and the proposed competency configuration still needs to be validated and is a research agenda for the future. Five conceptually distinct functions at the individual and workforce levels describe at which point protection may contribute to the decision pathway, but are not necessarily assumed to be empirically separable: recognize, interrogate, verify, contextualize, and escalate. Organizational capacity is limited to controls particular to created health information such as authorized sources, attainable human routing, incident monitoring and corrective action. Platform and regulatory conditions are constraints, safety, access, calibrated trust, and equity, outcomes. The framework was created using an expert guided purposive synthesis of the 62 sources that were retained, not a systematic review process. It distinguishes between an explanatory risk model and a normative control architecture and categorizes outputs with respect to type of output, severity, urgency, reversibility, context dependence, mitigation feasibility, and remaining risk. Falsification criteria are now included in six propositions. The candidate self-report indicators are kept as material for the cognitive interviewing only and must be correlated with behavioral vignettes before use for psychometric purposes. GenAI-HIR is therefore not a validated scale, certification standard or replacement for accessible professional care; it is a model for competency that can be falsified in future research and a governance structure that can be audited for current implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human rights have become a pervasive vocabulary in Indian legal and social science research, yet the structure and direction of this expanding literature have rarely been examined systematically. This review maps 457 Scopus-indexed journal articles on human rights with at least one Indian institutional affiliation, published between 2016 and 2026, using performance analysis and science-mapping techniques. Annual output grew more than five-fold, from 14 articles in 2016 to 75 in 2025 and 82 in 2026, a compound annual growth rate of about 20.5 per cent. The literature is highly dispersed: the 457 articles appeared in 318 journals, 36 of which account for one-third of the output, and 93 per cent of the 1,516 authors contributed only one article. Citation impact is modest (median one citation; 36.3 per cent uncited; dataset h-index 22). Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies six principal clusters: constitutional equality and discrimination; public health, pandemic and surveillance; artificial intelligence and intellectual property; climate change, displacement and the rights of nature; data protection and international law; and sustainable development and consumer protection. Thematic evolution shows a shift from trade-related intellectual property and health policy in 2016-2020 to COVID-19 and constitutional dignity in 2021-2023, and to artificial intelligence, data protection and climate change in 2024-2026. In contrast, the institutions through which rights are enforced receive very little attention: police, prisons and custody appear in about 2 per cent of articles, caste and Dalit concerns in 2.2 per cent, and the National Human Rights Commission in only three articles (0.7 per cent), none of which takes a commission as its object of study. The review argues that Indian human rights scholarship has undergone a “technological and regulatory turn” that risks neglecting the accountability of the coercive state, and proposes a research agenda centred on enforcement institutions, caste and gender intersections, and data-driven evaluation.

The introduction of innovative products is a critical driver of competitive advantage in highly turbulent technological environments. The objective of this article is to systematically analyze the recent literature on the marketing strategies that optimize the acceptance and performance of such innovations. Using a systematic-narrative methodology, a final corpus of 20 scientific articles published between 2020 and 2025 in high-impact databases such as Scopus and Web of Science was selected. The results reveal that commercial success does not reside exclusively in technical superiority, but in the creative configuration of an integrated marketing mix, where packaging design, dynamic pricing, and the diversification of channels toward e-commerce reduce adoption barriers. A strategic shift is identified, moving from traditional launch models toward agile, iterative, and niche approaches that prioritize user co-creation to mitigate perceived risk. Furthermore, functional communication and educational pre-announcements emerge as essential cognitive mechanisms for reducing consumer resistance to change in the face of radical innovations. It is concluded that dynamic organizational capabilities, enhanced by Marketing 4.0 and artificial intelligence, are crucial for personalizing the value proposition and ensuring product sustainability in global markets.

The development of digital technology has enabled the emergence and expansion of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs), which are transforming education through global accessibility, flexibility, and interactivity. This paper analyzes several platforms, their structure, the role of mentors, and the application of learning analytics. By searching citation databases and using generative artificial intelligence tools, relevant studies in the field were identified as the foundation of the analysis. An analysis of the most prominent MOOC platforms was conducted, with a more detailed comparison between the international platforms Coursera, edX, Future Learn, and the Croatian national platforms Srce and CARNET. The research shows that platforms differ in their use of technology, target groups, and approaches to mentorship, but they share a common goal: to provide accessible and personalized education. Personalized education is maintained through the role of mentors, reflected in communication on forums, AI assistants, and peer interaction. Learning analytics also play an equally important role, enabling precise monitoring of progress and adapting content to the specific needs of individuals. Alongside many advantages, the paper also discusses challenges such as privacy protection and data accuracy, which influence the development of MOOCs.

documents.abstract: This paper studies the local geometry of semantic meaning in large language models. Current representation analyses ask whether meanings are close in embedding space, or whether linear probes separate semantic classes, but they do not characterize the within-concept local geometry: what is invariant across realizations of a single semantic factor, what varies, and what changes when meaning is refined. This paper characterizes that geometry through two controlled probes evaluated on four architecturally diverse decoder-only LLMs (Gemma 4, Llama 3.2, Qwen 2.5, Pythia). A cross-lingual probe uses language as a perturbation to separate exact meaning matches, same-factor realizations, nearby concepts, and out-of-domain contrasts. A refinement probe separates specificity-bearing semantic narrowing from high-probability attributive elaboration and adversarial controls; both probes are validated by blind human judgments. Four findings recur across all models: under mean pooling, once dominant variance directions are removed, sentence pairs order by semantic relatedness (same factor, then same domain, then different domain) without overlap over a band of layers; semantic factors organize around an invariant core surrounded by structured realization-specific variation; refinement produces directed displacement into tighter neighborhoods, including against controls built on the same base noun; and sentence-level and token-local readouts expose complementary geometry (volume contraction at the sentence level, sharper anisotropic endpoints at token-local readout). We interpret these results as evidence that LLM semantics are organized as local anisotropic neighborhoods in which meaning contracts under refinement.
